title: Draft in depth
lead: Pressure, temperature and resistance: why a draft pours right, and how to find out why it doesn’t.

sections.name: Pressure, temperature, carbonation

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Temperature and gas pressure together set the fizz.

know: At 38°F, about 11 psi holds 2.5 volumes of CO2.
Warmer beer or less pressure: flatter. More pressure: fizzier.
sections.source: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org)

sections.name: A balanced system

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Pressure on the keg equals the resistance of the system.

know: Balanced draft pours about 2 oz a second.
Lifting beer up adds resistance; so does narrow line.
Fix the flow with line, never with gas.
sections.source: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org)

sections.name: Gas blends and nitro

lines.label: In short
lines.text: Long draws and nitro beers need nitrogen in the mix.

know: Nitro: 25/75 gas and a restrictor plate for the cascade.
sections.source: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org)

sections.name: Fixing a foamy pour
know: Temperature is the most common cause of draft problems.
Then: kinked line, worn washers, empty gas, dirty system.
Never compressed air in a keg.
sections.source: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org); Cicerone, US Certified Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 (cicerone.org)

keyPoints.line: or lower pressure: it goes flat.

read.bigIdea: The keg’s pressure has to match the beer.
read.where: **Carbonation** is measured in **volumes of CO2**: most beers sit at **2.2–2.8**. Temperature and gas pressure together hold it there. In the Brewers Association’s example, a keg at **38°F** needs about **11 psi** to keep **2.5 volumes**. Let it warm to 42°F at the same pressure and it slowly goes **flatter**; turn the gas up at 38°F and it gets **fizzier**. The right pressure depends on the bar’s temperature, altitude and the beer, so it’s set once and held steady.
read.mixup: Altitude changes the gauge reading too: add about 1 psi for every 2,000 ft above sea level.

read.bigIdea: Resistance slows the beer down to the right speed.
read.where: A **balanced** system applies exactly as much pressure as the system resists, and pours clear beer at about **2 oz a second** (about **8 seconds a pint**). Resistance comes from **gravity** (about half a pound for every foot the beer rises) and **friction** in the line: narrow **3/16-inch** line resists about **3 lb per foot**, wide barrier tubing almost none. Installers fine-tune with a short “choker” of narrow line. **Never** change the gas to speed up or slow down a pour: it over- or under-carbonates the beer and causes foam.
read.mixup: Turning the gas up for a faster pour makes the beer fizzier and foamier. Flow is fixed with line.

keyPoints.line: for nitro stout, through a restrictor plate.

read.bigIdea: Nitrogen lets you push hard without adding fizz.
read.where: Long-draw systems (over about **50 ft**) usually need **blended gas**: **nitrogen** barely dissolves in beer, so it adds pushing power without **overcarbonating**. Blenders used to default to 60/40; the Brewers Association now calls **70% CO2 / 30% N2** the default and says the best practice is to calculate your own. **Nitro** beers are low in CO2 and pushed with **25/75** gas through a faucet with a **restrictor plate** that knocks the nitrogen out into the cascading head. Put nitro gas on a regular beer and it goes **flat** in days; put pure CO2 on a nitro beer and it **overcarbonates**.
read.mixup: Nitro beer isn’t full of nitrogen. It’s low-CO2 beer with a little nitrogen, and the faucet makes the creamy head.

keyPoints.line: check it first: keg, then faucet.

read.bigIdea: Foam has a short list of causes.
read.where: The Brewers Association calls **temperature** the most common cause of draft problems: check the beer in the **keg**, then at the **faucet**. Then work the list: a **kinked** or wrong-size line, pressure **too high or too low**, worn **coupler or faucet washers**, a **dirty** system, a **leak or empty** gas tank, a torn keg valve seal, clogged faucet vents. Air compressors may only drive beer **pumps** or bag-in-keg systems, **never** a regular keg.
read.mixup: Foam isn’t always too much gas. Too little pressure causes foam too, as CO2 breaks out of the beer.

sources: Brewers Association, Draught Beer Quality Manual, 4th ed., 2019 (brewersassociation.org); Cicerone, US Certified Cicerone Syllabus v6.0 (cicerone.org). Checked Nov 8, 2026.
